ri_wolf_hill_quarry.blurb: Wolf Hill Quarry is an old abandoned quarry in Smithfield, Rhode Island, and it is mostly a winter destination. Once temperatures stay low, ice forms fairly dependably, with flows roughly 20 to 50 feet tall; the best lines hang near the back of the pit and need a solid cold spell to come in. The ice here runs from WI3 to WI5. A handful of boulder problems also exist, from V3 up, with one much harder outlier, but the quarry rock is loose and poor, so dry climbing is a secondary draw. It is a short walk from the road.

ri_lost_boulder_the.blurb: The Lost Boulder is a single big block tucked into the woods of Arcadia Management Area in southwest Rhode Island, a place that is mostly known for bouldering. Heights vary around the block, and the rock has good texture with slopers and incut flakes. It holds a dozen problems that span a wide range, from an easy V1 through the mid grades up to a few very hard lines at V10 and beyond. It is regarded as one of the better individual boulders in the state, and a cool, dry season is more pleasant than the buggy summer.

ut_old_crusty.blurb: Old Crusty is a small sandstone crag in the Indian Creek corridor of San Juan County, southeast Utah. Its roughly dozen climbs are all trad, and every one sits in the 5.10 range, so there is little here for beginners or for anyone chasing harder grades. It is a quieter option compared with the better-known Creek walls, and the route lines are on the shorter side, ideal for a mellow day of desert crack and corner climbing on the moderate end of the Indian Creek scale.

ut_angel_s_landing.blurb: Angels Landing is a huge sandstone buttress on the west side of Zion Canyon, with the Virgin River curving around its base. The climbing is long wall routes, both trad and aid, taking several to a dozen pitches. Free grades run from 5.8 into the low 5.13 range, though most lines sit between 5.8 and 5.11. The rock is fragile when damp, so a few dry days after rain matter here. A paved trail over the summit gives an easy walk-off, and spring and fall are the comfortable seasons in this desert climate.

ut_cragganzenden.blurb: Cragganzenden is a sport crag in the Right Fork of Maple Canyon, central Utah, tucked between Zen Garden and Cragganmore. Its dozen sport routes are on conglomerate cobble and cover a broad spread: a few easy-to-moderate leads in the 5.5 to 5.8 range, a run of 5.10s, and several 5.11s with a lone 5.12 at the top end. Exposures vary, so some lines catch morning sun, others the afternoon, and some stay sunny all day. A shady corridor keeps the belay spot cool, and the long moderates are well worth doing.
